newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Police vanish as Serb protesters march to centre.
newsitem.headline: Police vanish as Serb protesters march to centre.

text.p: Serbian police all but vanished as more than 5,000 pro-democracy demonstrators defied curbs on marches and swept from a Belgrade suburb into the city centre.

"This march is legal because the government is illegal," said Ognjen, a young man in his early 20s, as he and thousands of residents of the Banovo Brdo district braved freezing cold and marched eight km (5 miles) on Tuesday night to a rally.

For the past several weeks, Belgrade police have prevented marchers protesting against election fraud from interfering with traffic, and have on occasion clubbed demonstrators, but this time the police appeared to have given up.
The Banovo Brdo demonstrators, growing bolder after 10 weeks of pro-democracy protests across Serbia, blocked the district's main shopping street at about 7:30 p.m.

For the next two hours, the march blocked street after street, a main highway, and a traffic tunnel in the city centre until demonstrators reached the main rally organised by the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition in Republic Square.
There they hung flags and banners on a statue to the cheers and applause of some 60,000 people who turned out for speeches by the Zajedno leaders.
The only signs of police along the march route were a lone patrol car that stayed about a half km ahead and scurried away anytime the march came near, and two policemen at a snack bar.
"The police are gone because we are strong, like Mike Tyson," said Marko, a 17-year-old professional handball player who helped with crowd security and ran ahead to intersections to stop traffic.
"The police are gone today, and we are going into town."
The march snowballed as it went along, with people coming out of their homes to join and hundreds more cheering and blowing whistles on their balconies or from open windows as signs of support.
Cars from oncoming traffic tooted their horns and in one neighbourhood people threw newspaper confetti from balconies.
"This is a demonstration because the government is not good," said Milena, a woman in her 40s who marched into town with her husband.
"Why are the police gone? I think they are gone because they know they will lose -- and we will win," she said.

Other marchers said they thought they would win the test of wills with autocratic Socialist President Slobodan Milosevic, whose government annulled Zajedno victories in 14 cities in November elections, sparking the protest movement.
"We won the elections, you know, so the people of Belgrade are in the opposition," said teacher Ivan Peric.
"We have the intellectuals with us, the students, the universities. We have the United States with us and today Russia. So we will win...and will go on as long as it takes."
